bodyText:
If things haven't felt crazy enough, the government has now told families to prepare and keep three critical things at home. My brother who is former special forces told me to add a fourth.

I'm Jen. I'm 44. I live just outside Pensacola, Florida, with my husband Mike, our two kids, and a golden retriever who thinks the couch belongs to her.

Maddie is nine. Sam is six. Our life is school drop-offs, soccer practice, and a fridge covered in drawings nobody is allowed to throw away.

I'm not a prepper. I want to say that clearly, because I know how some of this is going to sound.

I don't watch end-of-the-world videos. I've never owned a bucket of freeze-dried anything. Until this month, our emergency plan was a flashlight in the junk drawer that may or may not have had batteries in it.

My brother Dan is the sensible one in our family. He moved to London twelve years ago for work. He lives there now with his wife and their two boys, and he works in insurance.

Dan reads the fine print on everything. He checks the tire pressure before every road trip. But he is not a worrier. He's the one who tells everyone else to calm down.

He thinks people who talk about the end of the world need a hobby.

So when he sent me a link on a Sunday night in late September, with no message at all, I almost didn't open it.

It was an interview with Britain's Defence Secretary.

The man in charge of Britain's entire military had sat down with one of their biggest newspapers. And he'd told ordinary families to keep three things in the house.

Some cash.

A supply of bottled water.

And some tinned food. Canned food, to us. The kind you can eat cold, "if your electric goes," as he put it.

He listed the reasons, one after another. Cyber attacks. Power cuts. Flooding. Wildfires. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

He said he wasn't trying to scare anyone. He said most people would have these things in the cupboard already. His exact words were "alert, not alarmed."

I read it twice, then texted Dan back. "That's a British thing," I wrote. "Different country, different problems."

He replied with one line. "It's not a British thing. Please just do it."

I didn't do it. I put a little heart on his message, made the kids' lunches for Monday, and forgot about it.

I want you to remember that part, because it's the part I think about most now.

Two weeks later, a storm called Isaias started building in the Gulf.

At first it looked like every other storm we get this time of year. The weather people drew the cone on the map. The kids asked if school would be closed. Mike went to fill up the car.

Then it got stronger. By Friday it was a hurricane, and it was heading for our stretch of coast.

Isaias came ashore near Destin on the night of Friday, October 9th, as a Category 2. We're not far from there.

I'll spare you most of that night. The wind sounds different when it's that strong. It doesn't howl. It roars, like a train that never finishes passing.

The kids slept in our bed, and the dog wouldn't leave the hallway. Around midnight, the power went.

By the next morning, more than 880,000 homes and businesses across Florida, Alabama and Georgia had no electricity. We were one of them.

Nobody I know got through that storm without a story. Four people didn't get through it at all.

I'm not going to pretend we had it worst. We didn't. Our roof held. Nobody was hurt.

But something happened that weekend that I wasn't ready for, and it's the reason I'm writing this.

It was the water.

I'd always thought of a hurricane as a wind problem. Board up the windows, bring in the patio chairs, wait it out.

I had never once thought of it as a water problem.

On Saturday the tap was still running. I filled the kettle without thinking, the way I always do, and then remembered the stove was electric.

On Sunday, the notice came through on a neighbor's phone, because ours were nearly dead. Boil water before drinking it. Our town was under a boil-water advisory.

Boil it with what, I thought.

Mike dug the camping stove out of the garage. It had one canister of gas left, about half full.

That's when I actually counted what we had.

Most of a case of the little bottles. A gallon jug in the fridge, already going warm. A couple of sports drinks the kids had forgotten about in the pantry.

Maybe three gallons. For four people and a dog. In the Florida heat. With no air conditioning.

We went through the first gallon by lunchtime. I wasn't even counting the dog's bowl.

Mike drove to the store on Sunday afternoon. The roads were full of branches and the traffic lights were out. He came home an hour later with nothing.

"No water," he said. "Not one case. People were buying sparkling water and juice and anything else that was wet."

I remember standing in the kitchen in the heat, looking at the bottles lined up on the counter, and doing a kind of math I'd never done before in my life.

Not money math. How many days.

Sam asked for a glass of water before bed that night. I gave him half a cup and told him to sip it slowly.

He's six, and he didn't understand why. I didn't want to explain it.

That night, with the kids finally asleep and the whole house silent, I opened Dan's message again.

"Please just do it."

I called him the next morning. In London it was already the afternoon.

"Are you okay?" was the first thing he said, because he'd been watching the storm on the news all weekend.

I told him we were fine. I told him about the water. I told him about the half cup.

He was quiet for a second. Then he said, "Did you do the three things?"

"No," I said. "I didn't think it applied to us."

"I did all three," he said. "And one more."

I asked him why. What made a man who rolls his eyes at everything take a politician's advice so seriously.

He told me it wasn't really the politician. It was that governments were all starting to say the same thing at the same time.

The European Union has been telling families to keep 72 hours of food and water at home since last year. Britain is launching a whole national campaign about it this autumn.

"When governments start telling people to keep water in the house," he said, "they're not guessing. They're planning. They just don't want to say it any louder than they have to."

"It isn't about war," he said. "It's about everything going wrong at once. A storm. A power cut. A cyber attack on the wrong system. You don't need the end of the world. You just need one bad week."

"And you just had yours," he said.

Then he explained the part I'd never understood.

Our tap water runs on electricity. Pumps push it through the pipes to every house. Treatment plants clean it. Computers control both.

When the power goes, the pumps can go with it. When the pumps go, the pressure drops. And when the pressure drops, dirty water can get into the pipes.

That's why the advisories come after storms. It isn't always a broken pipe. Sometimes it's just the power.

He sent me a story from the week before. Over on the other side of Florida, a storm knocked out power to the water pumps, the pressure dropped, and families were told to boil their water before drinking it.

No power. No pumps. No safe water. That's the whole chain, and it's only three links long.

Then he asked me a question I still think about.

"How long would your water have lasted if that advisory had gone on for two weeks?"

I didn't need the math. We'd barely made it through two days.

"Okay," he said. "Here's the number they don't put in the headline."

The British government's own guidance says a person needs 2.5 to 3 liters of water a day just to survive. That's drinking water only.

To drink, cook and keep clean, it says about 10 liters per person, per day.

We're a family of four. That's 40 liters a day. About ten and a half gallons. Every single day.

For three days, that's 120 liters. Over 30 gallons. Roughly five cases of gallon jugs stacked in the garage, just to get through a long weekend.

My three gallons wouldn't have lasted us until lunch on day one by that standard.

"That's the problem with bottled water," Dan said. "It's a countdown. Every bottle you open is one fewer. You can fill the garage and all you've done is buy a few more days. Then you're right back where you started."

He walked me through it the way he walks through everything. Like an insurance claim.

Option one. Buy more bottled water. It helps, and you should have some. But it's heavy, it fills the garage, and you can't take it with you if you have to leave. A week of water for a family our size weighs about 600 pounds.

Option two. Boil it. That works, as long as the power is on or the gas is on. Which is exactly the moment you don't have them.

Option three. Go to the store. We'd tried that.

"So what's the fourth thing?" I asked him.

He laughed. "I wondered when you'd ask. It isn't more water. It's a way to make more."

He keeps a small hollow-fiber water filter in the kitchen drawer. One in the car. One in each of his boys' school bags. Each one about the size of a flashlight.

"The three things get you through a few days," he said. "This is what you need when a few days isn't enough."

I'll be honest, my first reaction was the same as it had been to the article. A filter? Like the camping ones? So I sat down and read. The good portable filters use something called a hollow-fiber membrane.

Picture thousands of tiny straws packed side by side, each one thinner than a hair. The walls of those little straws are full of microscopic holes.

The holes are about 0.1 microns wide. That's so small that bacteria and parasites physically can't fit through. They get trapped on the outside. Clean water passes through to the inside.

To give you an idea of how small that is, a single E. coli bacterium is roughly one to two microns long. Giardia, a parasite that causes a lot of the stomach illness people get from untreated water, is around ten microns across. That's about a hundred times wider than the holes it would need to squeeze through.

It isn't a chemical killing anything. It's more like a sieve so fine that the things that make you sick simply can't get to the other side.

No chemicals. No electricity. No batteries. Just the size of the hole.

I asked Dan the obvious question. We already have a filter on the fridge, and a pitcher filter on the counter. Doesn't that do the same thing?

It doesn't. Most of those are carbon filters. They're designed to make tap water that's already been treated taste better, by taking out chlorine and odors. Most of them aren't designed to stop bacteria and parasites, and the fridge one doesn't work at all when the power's off.

That one honestly surprised me. I'd assumed we were already covered.

It's the same kind of technology used in field water filtration by aid organizations. The people who show up after floods and earthquakes, when the taps in a whole region have stopped.

You can drink straight through one like a straw. Or you can attach it to a bottle and squeeze the water through.

Which means almost any freshwater you can get to becomes drinking water. Rain in a bucket. A creek. A pond. The water still sitting in your pipes and your water heater.

I thought about that weekend. The rain barrel by Mike's shed was full to the top. The creek behind the kids' school was running high. We'd been surrounded by water the whole time.

We just couldn't drink any of it.

Using one is simpler than I expected. You fill the bag or bottle with water from wherever you are, screw the filter on, and squeeze or sip. When it starts to slow down, you push a little clean water back through it with a syringe to flush it out, and it flows again.

There's nothing to set up and nothing to plug in. Dan's youngest figured it out in about ten seconds, which tells you everything.

I also wanted to know what these filters can't do, because I don't trust anything that claims to do everything.

A filter like this is built for freshwater. It removes bacteria and parasites. It does not remove viruses, chemicals, or salt. It won't make seawater or a chemical spill safe. And if your water company tells you to boil, you still do what they say.

Honestly, that made me trust it more. It does one job. The exact job I needed done that weekend.

Dan told me which one he has. I looked at a few others too, because that's who I am now.

I went with the ClearX Pro from Standby Supply.

Here's why, and I'll keep it short.

According to the company, each one filters about 1,500 liters, roughly 400 gallons, of freshwater before it needs replacing. At the 3 liters a day the government says you need to survive, that's well over a year of drinking water for one person.

It weighs about two ounces. It doesn't need power or batteries. It doesn't expire sitting in a drawer. And it comes with a lifetime warranty.

Over 14,000 families have one.

The lifetime warranty mattered to me more than I expected. A company that's willing to stand behind something forever is telling you how long they think it'll last.

When the box arrived, I was surprised by how small it was. It fit in the palm of my hand. It's lighter than my phone.

And it cost less than our weekly grocery run.

Mike, I should say, rolled his eyes at all of this at first. Same as I had in September. He thinks I've been reading too much.

Then I reminded him about the store on Sunday afternoon. The empty shelves. The half cup.

He went quiet. The next day he asked me to order one for his truck.

Now compare one filter to what the government is telling families to store. Over 30 gallons of bottled water for three days. Five cases in the garage. All of them counting down.

One filter in a drawer doesn't count down. It just keeps going, for as long as there's freshwater to put through it.

That's the fourth thing. Not more storage. A way out of the countdown.

Here's what we did.

One in the kitchen drawer, next to the flashlight that now definitely has batteries in it.

One in the glovebox of each car.

One in each of the kids' backpacks.

And one in the hurricane box, which we now actually have.

The first weekend after they arrived, I took the kids out to the rain barrel by the shed.

Maddie filled a cup with rainwater. It had a leaf in it and a few bits floating around. She made a face at it.

Sam drank through the filter like it was a juice box. He said it tasted like nothing. Then he wanted to do it again.

They thought it was a science experiment. I let them think that.

Because the next time the power goes and the notice comes through, I don't want it to be the first time they've ever seen one. I want it to be normal.

I also did the three things. The cash is in an envelope in the safe. The canned food is on the bottom shelf of the pantry. And yes, we have bottled water now too.

The bottles are for the first few days. The filters are for everything after.

Then I thought about our mom.

She's 71. She lives on her own, about an hour from us, in a little house with a big garden she won't give up. She takes her pills every morning with a glass of water from the tap.

During the storm, I couldn't reach her for most of a day. The phones were down. When I finally got through, she told me she'd been drinking the water from the tap the whole time. She hadn't heard about the advisory.

She was fine. But I sat in my car afterward and shook.

Dan sent her one the same week. She keeps it in the kitchen drawer next to her tea towels, where she'll actually see it.

My neighbor across the street saw the box on our porch and asked what it was. I told her the whole story standing in the driveway. She ordered two before I'd finished.

That's the thing about going through a week like that. Afterward, everyone on your street suddenly has the same question you did.

A week after the storm, I watched the news from France on my phone.

More than half a million people in the streets in a single day. Over a thousand arrests. Shops broken into in Paris, Marseille, Nice, and city after city.

I'm not saying that's coming here. I don't think it is.

But it reminded me of something Dan said on the phone. Normal doesn't end with a warning. It ends on an ordinary Friday night, when the wind picks up and the lights go out.

I hope Isaias is the worst storm we ever see. I hope the power stays on and the water stays clean. I hope the people in charge of Britain's defence are just being careful.

But the people whose job it is to plan for the worst are telling families to keep water at home. I lived through why.

Hope isn't a plan. Half a cup of water for a six-year-old isn't a plan either.

The man who rented Cabin 6 from me two weeks ago paid for three nights in cash, wrote a first name on my registration card that was not the one on his driver's license, asked me on Wednesday what runs the pump on our well, and on Thursday night, out on my office porch, told me who signs his paycheck. Four days on our place and I never once saw a phone in his hand. Never asked for the WiFi password. Walked down to the creek by himself every evening about sundown and just stood there. I have not told a soul what he said to me that Thursday, not even at church. I'm typing it out now because everything that has been on the news since he left goes right back to that question he asked me about my well.

Dale and I have rented out these six cabins for nineteen years.

You hand enough strangers a key and you get to where you can size one up before the car door shuts. The fly fisherman who is going to lie about what he caught. The couple up for their anniversary who aren't speaking. The widower who books the same cabin every October and does not want to be asked why.

After nineteen years I don't work at it. It just happens.

I knew Glenn was something else before he got to my counter.

Tuesday, a little before noon. He came up our gravel alone in a plain white sedan and parked at the far end of the lot, not by the office door like everybody does.

One bag. A green canvas duffel gone soft at the corners.

He stopped in the office doorway before he said a word. Looked at the map of the property I keep on the wall, the one with the cabins and the creek and the road out. Like a man counting doors.

Around sixty. Trim. Reading glasses on a cord. Yes ma'am, no ma'am. Didn't ask how the fishing was. Didn't take a brochure for the caverns. Didn't ask where a person gets supper around here.

Cash. Three nights. Counted it out in twenties.

I ask every guest for a license for the file. The one he slid across said Thomas. The card he filled out said Glenn.

I let it lie.

Then he took the key, drove down to Cabin 6 and backed that car in behind it so the plate faced the woods.

In nineteen years nobody has paid me cash for three nights. Nobody has written down a name that wasn't his while I stood there holding the proof. And nobody has ever come to stay on a fishing creek without a rod.

By Wednesday suppertime I had swallowed about six questions I would normally have asked out loud.

Thursday night, a quarter to ten. Dale had gone up to the house at eight, he gets up at four-thirty. I was on the office porch folding cabin towels with the screen door propped so I could hear the little TV on the counter.

Glenn was in the other rocker on his second beer.

He had been there since before dark. Hardly a word. Looking out at where the creek is. You can't see it from there at night. You can only hear it.

The news gave Iran about half a minute. Gas up thirteen cents in a week, national average four twenty-seven. One sentence about talks. Then the weather.

Glenn listened to it through the screen. Never turned his head.

When the weather map came up he said, more to the beer can than to me, "Half a minute. They have got it down to half a minute."

I quit folding.

I said, "What is that supposed to mean."

He took his time.

He said, "Nothing. Thinking out loud."

I said, "You have been here three days and I bet you haven't said twenty words to me. You've sat on my porch two hours tonight and not asked me one thing about myself, which I promise you is a record for that chair. A man that quiet finally says something, I want to hear the rest of it."

He looked right at me for the first time since he checked in.

He said, "You watch that every night?"

I said, "Every night."

He said, "How does it leave you feeling?"

I said, "How does it leave me feeling."

He said, "The Iran part. Ceasefire. No ceasefire. Paper signed. Strait shut again. What are you left with when it goes to the weather."

I had to think about it.

I said, "Like I have seen it already. Like it's a rerun. April they had a ceasefire. June President Trump signed that Islamabad paper with Iran's president and three days later the strait was closed again. I quit trying to keep it straight. Last week I got up and started the dishwasher right in the middle of it."

He nodded one time.

He said, "That is what it's for."

I waited.

I said, "What what's for."

He drank. Set the can on the porch rail.

He said, "I ought not to. I don't know you and I don't know who you'd tell. But you caught it when I said it. Mostly people don't. And I have not said any of this out loud to anybody outside my building since March."

He looked at the can.

He said, "I work for the Energy Department. Emergency planning. I write the long papers on what happens over here if that strait stays shut."

He looked up.

He said, "I should not have said that. I'd take it kindly if you forgot it."

I said, "Glenn."

He said, "Yeah."

I said, "You paid me cash."

He said, "Yeah."

I said, "Your license says Thomas."

He said, "It does."

I said, "You backed your car in so nobody can read the plate from the road."

He said, "Yeah."

I said, "And yesterday you asked me what runs my well pump."

He said, "I know I did."

I set the towel down.

I said, "What is going on."

He looked out at the dark a good while.

Then he looked back at me.

---

He said, "What they tell you about Iran is true as far as it goes. It just quits halfway. Every night. On purpose."

I waited.

He said, "The half you get is the cover for the half you don't."

I said, "The half I don't being what."

He took a drink.

He said, "Look how it runs. April, ceasefire. Ten days on, Iran shuts the strait again. May, the Navy starts escorting ships. June, Trump and Pezeshkian sign the memorandum and everybody lets their breath out. Three days. Shut again. July the truce comes apart. August the Navy says it has cleared better than a hundred suspected mines, and that sounds like headway. It is the middle of September and that water is still shut."

He looked at me.

He said, "You felt it tonight. I watched you. 'It's a rerun.' Now put that in every living room in the country, every night, for six months."

A drink.

He said, "Folks who notice get tired. Tired folks quit keeping track. Folks who quit keeping track quit asking the one question my office would rather not get asked on camera."

He set the can down.

I said, "Which is what."

He looked at me.

He said, "What a closed strait does to your house."

I said, "The strait is on every single night."

He said, "The strait is on every single night. The map. The little ship pictures. The reporter in the vest. You have heard the word Hormuz more since March than in all your life before it."

He looked out at the dark.

He said, "What you have not heard, not one time, is what it means for a woman with six cabins and a well if it stays shut through the winter."

I waited.

He said, "That half never airs. The strait gets the map and the man in the vest. Your kitchen, your daughter's kids' school, the hospital in town, they get nothing."

I said, "So what does it do."

He took a drink.

He said, "A fifth of the oil in the world goes through that water in a normal year. Twenty million barrels a day. The man who runs the International Energy Agency called this the largest supply disruption in the history of the oil market. On the record, his words. The rich countries drained four hundred million barrels out of their emergency tanks last spring, the most they ever have, and oil is over a hundred dollars anyway. The Philippines declared a national energy emergency in March. Slovenia started rationing gas the day before that, fifty liters a day to a driver. That's Asia and Europe, so you got it for one evening if you got it at all."

He looked at me.

He said, "It comes here. I could not tell you the week."

He took a drink.

He said, "Forget gasoline a minute. Think about diesel. Diesel is the truck that carries the treatment chemicals to your town's water plant. Diesel is the backup generator at the pump station. Diesel is the crew that comes out to fix the line. When diesel gets short and gets dear, all the slack goes out. Nothing breaks that day. It's that the next time something does break there is nothing standing behind it."

He set the can down.

He said, "Watch for the word 'voluntary.' Voluntary conservation. After that, 'advisory.' After that a schedule with your county's name on it. That is the order I would bet on, and I get paid to bet on it."

He looked at me.

He said, "And here is the piece nobody is going to hand you when it gets here."

I waited.

He said, "Who goes without has already been written down. I have read it. In January the Department signed an emergency order for Texas. In May it signed another one, for the grid that runs thirteen states and D.C. They spell out how the big data centers get pushed onto their own generators as the last step before the rolling blackouts start. Those orders are public. Nobody read them."

He looked at me.

He said, "Somebody has already sat down and worked out what order things get switched off in. There is a list. Your kitchen faucet is not on anybody's list. Nobody ever wrote a paper about your well."

He let that sit.

He said, "So when it comes they will call it a freak thing. A bad week. A once in a lifetime storm. They will call it that the next time too."

I didn't say anything for a while.

He took a drink.

He said, "Tired is what they are after. I've sat in the meetings where my long version gets boiled down to the short one. A tired country does not look underneath anything. By the time your lights flicker you will have been told for a year that it's all nearly settled."

I didn't say anything for a long time.

---

He took another long drink.

He said, "A lot of people in this country figure they are getting ready for something. Canned goods. Silver. Gas cans. Guns, ammunition. A generator from the home center, still in the box."

He looked at me.

He said, "Nearly every one of them skipped the first thing."

I waited.

He said, "Water."

I said, "Water."

He said, "Water."

He took a drink.

He said, "Nobody on that TV is going to say it. You turn the handle, it comes out. Been that way every day of your life. Mine too. A person can't hardly picture it any other way."

He looked at me.

He said, "Water is the first thing to go when the power runs short."

I waited.

He said, "Every treatment plant runs off the power company. Every pump station. Every pump between the river and somebody's sink. And you, you are on a well. Two hundred eighty feet, electric pump, you told me so yourself. The power drops, you've got what's sitting in the pressure tank and that's all you have got."

He stopped a second.

He said, "Texas. February of 2021. The grid went down in a freeze, and by that Saturday fourteen million people in a hundred and ninety counties had their water fouled up. A hundred and fifty thousand had none at all. Better than two thousand water systems put out boil notices and some of those ran past a month. The head of the state's own environmental agency said it plain. 'My family, my dog, my eight chickens are on day four without water at my house.'"

He looked at me.

He said, "That was weather. Nobody did that to them. Richmond, Virginia, January of last year. One power outage at the water plant. One. The valves could not close without power, the low rooms took on six feet of water inside ten minutes, and the city and three counties around it boiled their water the better part of a week."

He let that sit.

He said, "What I write papers about is not one cold snap and it is not one plant."

I let that sit too.

I said, "We would drive to town and buy water."

He said, "You and everybody. Austin, Texas, 2018. Boil notice. The shelves were bare in hours. The grocery chain down there ran better than a hundred trailers of water in one day to catch up, and that was one city with every truck in Texas free to come help. Now picture every city the same week, and the trucks short on diesel."

He looked at me.

He said, "You have grandkids."

It was not a question. He had seen the crayon fish taped up in my office window.

I said, "Three. The oldest is eleven."

He said, "Some evening about a week into it the littlest one is going to ask you for a drink. And you are going to be standing in your own kitchen with a dry faucet and nothing to hand her."

He looked at me.

He said, "That is the evening to get ready for. Forget the war and the memorandum and the map with the ships on it. A child and an empty cup. Nobody on TV is going to walk you up to that one ahead of time."

I didn't say anything.

---

He took another long drink.

He said, "The people I work with are fixed for it."

I waited.

He said, "Two men in my section squared their houses away in March, the week the strait closed. My deputy did hers in June and never said a word. I only know because her husband told my wife at a cookout. There is a retired Army engineer who consults for us and he has been set since the Texas freeze. None of them talk about it at work. None of them are scared either. They have just decided they are not going to be the one standing in that kitchen."

He looked at me.

He said, "Yesterday. The well."

I said, "Yeah."

He said, "I was not making conversation. I was checking."

I said, "Checking what."

He said, "Whether you had ever thought about it. Somebody who has thought about it answers different. They tell you about the hand pump, or the tank, or the spring up the hill. You told me two hundred eighty feet, electric pump, never gave you a day's trouble. Like I'd asked if it looked like rain. So I knew."

He set the can down.

He said, "Right now you are thinking this is for the bunker crowd. The fellas on cable with the freeze-dried buckets. You are about to tell me you're not a prepper."

I was, too. I had my mouth open to say it.

He said, "That part works best of all. Long as getting ready looks like something only odd people do, regular people won't do it. Then it comes, and the only ones who were ready are the handful everybody laughed at."

He looked at the can.

He said, "It all pushes the same direction. The rerun. The being tired. Half a minute and then the weather. It all leaves you sitting still. So when it does come you are sitting right where you were."

He took a drink.

He said, "Power is the handle. The power goes and the water goes with it. The water goes and you are not running your own house anymore. When the kids drink, when you cook, when you wash, whether the commode flushes, every bit of it waits on whoever decides when the lights come back. You have never had one day without that say-so, so you never noticed you had it."

He looked at me.

He said, "What you want is something that takes that handle out of their hand ahead of time. Water that comes whether the power does or it doesn't. Something that is in your house this week."

He set the can down.

He said, "And I do not mean a bunker. I don't mean a pallet of army meals or a generator or a cistern. I mean a tube. About nine inches long. Rides in a coat pocket. Anybody can own one and anybody can work one."

He moved the can over. Put his hand flat on his jacket pocket and left it there.

---

I said, "A tube."

He didn't answer for a bit.

He said, "I ought not show you."

I said, "You already told me."

He looked out at the dark again, where the creek was going by.

He said, "Yeah."

He took it out of his jacket. Held it in his lap a second.

He said, "You keep this to yourself. Dale included. Until you have made up your mind what you are going to do about any of it."

I said all right.

He set it on the arm of my rocker.

A plain tube about nine inches long.

I picked it up.

More to it than it looked. Solid.

I said, "What is it."

He said, "A filter."

I turned it over.

I said, "A filter for what."

He said, "Water."

I said, "That's all."

He said, "That's all."

I waited.

I could tell he was done volunteering.

I said, "How does it work."

He looked at his jacket. Then at the tube.

He said, "Threads onto a water bottle. Any regular one. The empties in your recycling."

I said, "And then."

He said, "Then you drink through it. Or you lay down on the bank and drink straight out of the creek with it, if it came to that. Or you hang the bottle upside down and let it drip into a pot."

I said, "And what comes out."

He said, "Water you can drink."

I said, "What's inside it."

He looked at me a second.

He said, "Two stages in one straw. First a membrane with holes one hundredth of a micron across. Bacteria will not fit through a hole that size. Parasites won't either. Then a carbon stage. The carbon is for chemicals and sediment."

I held it up to the porch light like that would tell me something.

I said, "Any water."

He said, "Any fresh water. Creek. Pond. Rain barrel. A bathtub you filled before the storm got there. Not the ocean. It won't take out salt."

I said, "How long is one good for."

He said, "Eighteen hundred gallons."

I said, "That doesn't mean a thing to me."

He said, "The government's own emergency page tells you to figure a gallon a person a day. So call it close to five years for one person."

I said, "And then."

He said, "Then you get another one. But it does not go bad sitting. No expiration date on it. Leave it in a drawer ten years."

I said, "What do you plug it into."

He said, "Nothing. No batteries. No pump. You are drinking through a tube."

I turned it over again.

I said, "This is what the people you work with have."

He looked at the dark.

He said, "It's what I have. There is one in my daughter's glovebox and she doesn't know it's in there."

I waited.

I said, "Show me."

He looked at me.

He said, "Ma'am, I drove nine hours to sit by a creek and not talk to anybody. I did not come here to put on a demonstration."

I said, "I want to see it work."

He looked at the dark again. Then he got up. Slow, the way you do when your knees have a say.

He said, "You got a flashlight."

He went down to the creek with my flashlight and the plastic pitcher I make sun tea in. I watched the light bob. He didn't dip from the middle where it runs clear. He went down by the low-water crossing where the neighbor's cows come through, and he came back with a pitcher the color of weak coffee. Bits of leaf in it. Something in there was swimming.

He fished an empty water bottle out of my recycling tub, the grocery store kind.

Poured the creek water in.

You could see the trash floating in it.

Threaded the tube onto the top.

Tipped the whole thing up over one of my jelly glasses.

It came slow. A thin stream.

Clear.

He held the glass up to the porch light.

Clear. Nothing floating. No color to it at all.

He handed it to me.

I am not going to lie to you. I stood there holding it.

He didn't push.

I drank it.

No taste. No grit. No creek. It tasted like a glass of water at my own sink on any morning of my life.

Just water.

I looked at the pitcher. Then the glass. Then Glenn.

I said, "That is the creek."

He said, "Yeah."

I said, "From below where the cows cross."

He said, "Yes ma'am."

Glenn unthreaded the tube and held it out to me.

He said, "Keep it."

I took it.

I walked up to the house at eleven with that tube in my cardigan pocket.

I did not sleep.

---

Friday morning Dale was at the kitchen table with his coffee and the farm report on.

I came in and set the tube down beside his cup.

He looked at it. Looked at me.

He said, "What's that."

I told him. All of it.

He said I'd been had.

Said a fella drinks two beers on a porch and all of a sudden he's with the government, he has heard that one before. Said I watch too much news and he has been telling me so since spring.

I got my boots on and went down to the creek.

Same pitcher. Same spot. The cows were standing in it this time.

I did the whole thing in front of him. Bottle out of the recycling, brown water in, leaves and all. Tube on top. Tipped it over a jelly glass and set the glass down by his coffee.

He looked at me.

He looked at the pitcher.

He looked at the glass.

He drank it.

Dale did not say anything for a good minute. For Dale that isn't unusual, but this was a different kind of quiet.

He picked up the pitcher and held it to the window. Set it down.

Picked up the tube. Turned it over twice. Set it down.

Then he said, real low, "He tell you where a person gets these?"

---

Glenn pulled out Saturday morning before six.

He came up to the office with the one duffel. Paid me cash for the extra night. Asked whether I aimed to do something with what he had told me or just think about it.

I told him do.

He nodded one time. Put the duffel on the back seat. Went down our gravel slow enough he didn't raise any dust.

I haven't heard from him. I don't expect I will.

That was nine days ago.

In those nine days.

Friday, the morning after that porch, drones shut down Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline. That is the main way to move oil out overland, around the strait. I only know because I went looking.

Sunday a ship was struck in the strait, and the word was the talks with Iran were not starting back up. Eight ships made it through that whole day. Before all this it was eighty-five a day.

Wednesday. Wichita, Kansas. About five in the morning the main water plant and pump station lost power. The plant was already running on its backup generators on account of a storm, and the generators quit. It was out about forty-five minutes. The pressure fell, and around half a million people, one out of every six people in Kansas, were told to boil their water. Some grade schools closed. The radio station there ran a picture of the water shelves at a grocery store, empty. The last piece of that system did not get cleared until Sunday afternoon.

Forty-five minutes.

Friday, Duluth, Minnesota. Power outage, pressure dropped, boil notice.

Iran's parliament speaker says the strait "will remain closed until Iran's conditions are met." Three hundred seventy-two ships are sitting out there going nowhere. Oil is a hundred and three dollars.

Saturday night I watched all of it get its half a minute and I thought about what he said. It's a rerun. Folks who notice get tired. Tired folks quit keeping track. Folks who quit keeping track quit asking.

And I thought about how I answered him about my well. Like he had asked me if it looked like rain. And what that told him about people like me.

That tube has been in my purse eleven days.

Dale ordered ten of them. Two of the five-packs. One five-pack for our daughter Shelby's house, which is her, Travis and the three kids. He did not tell me.

I know because the order confirmation came to the cabin email, and because there is a feed store receipt on the refrigerator now with all that written on the back in his block letters. He saw me reading it. He poured himself another cup and went out to the shop.

That is how a man changes his mind in this house. He makes a list.

---

If you have been watching the news since spring and feeling like it's a rerun, a deal and then no deal, the strait open and then shut, and you've caught yourself getting up to start the dishwasher in the middle of it, I did too. I don't believe anymore that feeling comes from nowhere.

They need you worn out. They need you sick of it. They need you looking at that map every night without one person telling you what it does to your own house if the strait stays shut another month. You get the map. You get the ships. You never get the arithmetic.

I personally checked in half the thirty-one families we woke up at three in the morning.

Handed them maps, pointed them to the swimming hole, told them which mornings the elk come down.

I never once said the word flood to a single one of them.

That night the river took the only road out from under all of them while they slept, and the warning system in our canyon turned out to be my father's flashlight and my bathrobe.

We knocked on every door ourselves, in the storm, some of them twice.

Nobody called us either.

That's the part I can't get past.

The rain gauge upstream knew before all of us did, and there's no telephone attached to it.

A boy with one shoe and his barefoot little sister reached the station with wet clothes and nowhere warm to lie down.

The first thing my father brought back from the lower campground was their brass cabin key, hanging from a branch above the road with the tag still tied to it, while the river carried picnic tables through the trees below.

He held it out to me at the ranger station and said the cabin was empty.

The family had made it uphill, but the key had stayed behind.

I was twenty-seven and had checked that family into the cabin that afternoon.

The boy had one shoe when he climbed into the truck.

His little sister had none.

By the time they reached the station, both children were sitting under the lights with wet clothes and nowhere warm to lie down.

That was the part of the evacuation nobody had put on a list.

My parents run a campground beside a river that comes down through a narrow valley.

The lower sites are pretty in the daytime.

There are trees over the picnic tables, pale stones along the bank, and a gravel road that follows the water before it climbs to the ranger station.

I work the office.

I answer the phone, write the names on the reservation cards, hand people their keys, and tell them where the bathhouse is.

That day, thirty-one families checked in.

The family in cabin seven had a boy around six and a little girl who kept losing one of her shoes.

They spent the afternoon near the water with their parents.

The river was low enough that my father could see the fire ring below the office.

The weather radio called for scattered storms.

We had heard that phrase all summer.

It usually meant a wet walk to the car and a night of rain on the roof.

By dark, water was running through the ditch beside the cabins.

In the middle of the night, every cabin door was shut and families were asleep inside.

The upstream rain gauge had no way to call the station, and our radio signal kept fading.

Then my father heard the river change.

It had grown louder and closer, even before he could see the water.

He took a flashlight down the campground road to find out what had happened.

When he called the office, his voice had changed.

"Wake the cabins," he said.

"Get everybody uphill."

The bridge below us was gone, and the road out had turned to water.

My mother took the cabin list.

I took the keys.

No warning was coming from outside the campground.

We carried it door to door in the rain.

At each door, I told people the road was gone and they had to come uphill.

People came out with children, medicine, shoes, and whatever they could carry in one trip.

One couple left their cooler on the porch.

An older woman carried one shoe in a grocery bag while her niece held her arm.

The girls in cabin three asked whether they could bring the stones they had collected.

Their father said yes, then put the stones down when he realized the medicine bag was more important.

At cabin seven, the boy opened the door before I knocked twice.

His parents were pulling jackets from a duffel.

His sister had found one shoe beneath the bunk and was trying to put it on with a wet sock.

I told the family to come uphill.

The father picked up the little girl, the boy grabbed his mother's hand, and we moved before the water came across the driveway and cut off another bag.

The truck ahead of us started up the switchback.

We put the family into the third truck because it still had room for their knees and the children.

The missing shoe stayed below.

The father kept looking down through the rear window as if the river might hand it back.

It didn't.

The trucks climbed slowly because water crossed the road in three places.

Branches fell across the lane.

My father and two other men got out and moved one while the families waited inside.

Everybody was wet by the time we reached the ranger station.

The station had lights because a generator was running.

It had coffee because the ranger had kept one burner going.

It did not have a warm room for thirty-one families.

The door opened every few minutes and sent wind across the floor.

The children sat on benches and concrete.

Their parents stood between them and the draft.

The family from cabin seven had a shoe full of river water and clothes that were wet through.

His mother asked whether the station had a laundry room.

She was still asking about the shoe because a dry shoe was the next answer she could see.

I didn't have one.

She took off her own socks and wrapped one around her daughter's foot.

The sock was wet soon after.

The ranger brought out towels.

They helped with dripping hair and hands, but they could not make soaked clothes dry in a room with no heat.

The generator kept the lights on.

The concrete kept pulling warmth from the children sitting on it.

Tessa was the search-and-rescue ranger on duty.

She opened the metal cabinet beside the radio and found a first-aid tin, rain covers, and hand warmers.

Rain covers kept more water off the outside of a coat, while the clothes underneath stayed wet, and the hand warmers had gone cold.

Tessa looked at the children and then at the door.

She asked me to move the benches away from the draft.

We did.

That helped the wind a little.

It did not change the cold under the children or the wet fabric against their bodies.

The boy stopped talking.

His mother put her hand on his cheek.

Tessa went back into the cabinet and reached behind the first-aid tin.

She brought out a folded green pouch.

The material inside was green on one side and silver on the other.

It was thin and flat, with small folds that caught the station light.

Tessa opened it on the bench and showed the boy's father how to place his son inside.

She kept his head clear.

She drew the lower edge around his legs and checked his hands.

Then she opened another for the little girl.

Each child had a separate layer around the warmth that child was already making.

The mother sat beside them and touched both green edges.

The boy asked if it was a tent.

Tessa told him it was an emergency heat shelter.

She said the body was the source of the heat.

Wet clothing, moving air, and cold ground were the paths that carried it away.

The shelter gave that heat fewer places to go.

She said soaked fabric, moving air, and cold surfaces could all carry warmth away from a body, even while the body was still making its own heat.

She was talking about soaked clothing in an exposed place where the dry-room comparison did not apply.

The explanation stayed with me because the generator was already working.

Coffee sat hot in the urn, and the trucks had already carried everybody uphill.

What we lacked was something that held a person's own warmth while the next safe step was being arranged.

Tessa said search teams and ambulance crews carry this kind of emergency shelter for people who come out of water or have to wait on cold ground.

She said the technology behind the reflective inside came from the same work developed for astronauts.

The product was called TerraShell.

It is an emergency thermal bivy that helps reflect body heat back toward the person and helps block wind, moisture, and the cold pull of the ground.

It does not need a battery, a charger, fuel, or a running engine.

The body is the source.

The TerraShell helps keep the warmth close.

That was why it worked for the part after the evacuation.

Road clearing, rides home, and the lower turn remained unfinished; the children still needed a better place to wait.

The boy stopped asking about his shoe, his sister fell asleep with one finger against the silver inside, and their parents kept watch beside the bench.

Tessa checked the openings and kept the children away from the door.

She used the shelter as one piece of care, not as a promise that the rest of the emergency had disappeared.

That was the first time I understood the category.

The pouch belonged in emergency gear for the hours nobody plans for.

An evacuation can end the danger and still leave people cold and waiting.

I didn't buy TerraShell because I wanted a room full of supplies.

I'm not a prepper.

I'm the campground host's daughter who keeps the names straight and calls my parents on Sundays.

I wanted something small enough to stay in the office, the car, or the drawer beside the back door.

The pouch is close to the size of a soda can when folded.

It weighs almost nothing.

It opens flat, with the green side facing the conditions and the reflective inside facing the person.

I practiced opening one on the living-room floor because the calm time is when you learn where the opening is.

It asks for no battery test, fuel rotation, or charge to remember.

You put it away and forget about it until a wet road, broken-down car, storm shelter, or powerless room gives you a reason to find it.

The family bundle made sense when I counted people rather than houses: one for my father, one for my mother, one for my sister's car, and one for each child who might be traveling with them.

Everybody gets their own shelter because a family is not one body sharing one layer.

That was what I saw on the bench at the station.

The boy needed his space.

His sister needed hers.

Their parents needed both hands available to care for them.

I can't tell you what happened in every home that owns one, and I won't make up a story for anybody else.

I can tell you why the product made sense to me.

She had her daughter Nora with her, rain on the windshield, and no idea how long the county truck would take.

Claire opened two pouches from the back of the car, one for herself and one for Nora, and kept both openings clear while they waited.

Nora stopped asking when the road would open long enough to eat the crackers Claire had packed.

When the tree was moved, Claire folded the pouches into the car and drove home to make the dinner she had planned.

That ordinary dinner was the part I remembered.

The wait had stayed difficult, but it had not taken the rest of the evening from them.

The families left in different cars once the upper route opened.

His sister carried her green pouch until her mother took it from her at the parking lot.

The campground is open again now.

The fire ring was rebuilt higher up.

My father checks the gauge more often.

My mother keeps the cabin list beside the radio.

I keep the green pouches where a hand can find them, hope the next storm is only rain on the roof, and know a family can leave the dangerous place with a long, cold wait ahead.

bodyText:
My neighbour's husband came back from a work trip to Whitehall last month and started quietly shutting his family's life down. Sold the narrowboat he spent six years doing up. Cancelled the Norwegian fjords cruise for their 35th anniversary. Took cash out of the bank. A lot of it. Talked his son into bringing the grandkids back from Spain. His wife was sure a consultant had given him bad news and he was keeping it from her. He told me the real reason over our back fence, and it came down to one word. That was five weeks ago. I still haven't told my husband. But I've quietly done every single thing he told me to do, before the rest of this road works it out.

His name is Graham.

61 years old. Thirty-four years in the electricity networks. Control rooms, mostly. The steadiest man I know.

I've lived next door to Graham and Linda for 14 years. Our grandkids run through the same sprinkler.

Graham goes Monday and comes back Thursday. Warrington mostly. This year, a lot of London. Whitehall.

Doesn't say much. Waves from the mower. You ask him something, you get the answer and nothing extra.

In 14 years I have not once seen that man rattled.

So when he started acting odd in August, I noticed.

First it was the boat.

Then the cruise. Linda had that brochure stuck on her fridge since Christmas.

Then the bank. She found the withdrawal slips in his jacket pocket.

Then a van pulled up from Stansted. Their son Daniel, his wife, two little girls and the dog. Into the spare rooms "for a while." Nobody would tell her why.

Then the deliveries started. Plain brown boxes. A whole pallet one time. Straight into his shed with the door pulled to behind him.

Linda sat at my kitchen table on a Wednesday and cried.

"He's ill. I know he's ill. He's had some kind of news and he's putting his affairs in order and he won't tell me."

I didn't know what to say to her.

Then Saturday morning I was at the sink, looked out of my kitchen window, and saw Graham doing something I have never seen him do in 14 years.

He was splitting logs.

Two tonnes at least, tipped beside his shed. Graham out there in his old jumper with a maul, swinging.

Graham and Linda have a gas fire. They've had a gas fire since the day they moved in.

He'd been at it the best part of an hour. No radio. No gloves. Just swinging.

I stood there and watched him a good 20 minutes.

Then I made two teas and walked out to the fence.

"Graham."

He stopped.

"Brought you a tea."

He looked at the maul. Looked at the pile. Looked at me.

Then he leaned the maul on the chopping block and came over.

"Thank you."

"Graham, what on earth are you doing?"

"Getting some logs in."

"Logs."

"Yep."

"For the gas fire."

"Log burner's being fitted Thursday."

I laughed. He didn't.

"Graham. Come on now."

"It's a stove. People have stoves. It's no big thing."

"A box of candles is no big thing. You've got a timber yard back there."

I nearly got a smile out of him.

"Linda thinks I've lost the plot."

"Linda thinks you're dying. She sat at my table on Wednesday and cried about it."

That one got to him. He looked down into his mug.

"I know. She asked me straight out that night."

"She thinks you've got six months and you won't tell her, Graham."

"I know."

"So what is it really."

Nothing. He drank some tea. Looked off past his shed at the trees at the bottom of the gardens.

I waited.

"You know I can't talk about work."

"I didn't ask about work."

"Anything I've got to say right now is work."

I kept my mouth shut.

"I've sat in a lot of rooms since the spring. That's all it is."

"All right."

"A few of them I'd have paid good money not to be in."

I came at it another way.

"Graham. What are you getting ready for?"

That one he felt.

He let out a long breath.

"You been following the oil thing? The strait?"

"Hormuz. Course. Petrol's daft money again. It's all anybody talks about in the queue at the Co-op."

He nodded slowly.

"That's the bit you're allowed to watch."

"Meaning what."

"Meaning the news shows you the ships. The rooms I've been in aren't about ships. They're about what gets done here, at home, once things get tight enough. None of that's been on your telly."

"What gets done."

He went quiet again.

Then: "You remember 2020?"

"Which part."

"The part where somebody decided which shops were essential. Where they told you how many people could sit round your own table at Christmas. Where three weeks turned into a year."

"I remember."

"Well, they kept the binder. All of that got built once and nobody took it apart."

I went cold right down both arms.

"Kept it for what."

"For this. Same binder. New reason."

"Graham."

"Fuel goes first. They won't call it rationing. Hospitals, emergency services, food lorries first. You and me get what's left and a queue to stand in."

"That doesn't happen here."

"It did happen here. The three-day week. You and I are both old enough to remember our mums doing tea by candlelight. And 2021, when the forecourts ran dry and they had the army driving the tankers. And it's happening right now. The government's own National Security Strategy says we have to 'actively prepare for the possibility of the UK homeland coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario.' Their words, not mine. We're not at the front of the queue. But we're in it."

"Okay."

"Then the lorries. Diesel goes where they say it goes. Shelves get thin, then patchy."

"Okay."

"Then the power. They've got a word for it. Rota disconnections. Your postcode goes off for three hours, then the next one does. Kindly don't put the kettle on between four and seven."

"Graham."

"And 2020 had an end because a virus runs its course. This one runs until the ships move. They've been attacking tankers in and around that strait since the start of the year. The Royal Navy's lot keep putting out warnings. There was a ship hit sixteen miles off Oman in September. The interim deal in June left the traffic well below normal and it's still well below normal. A fifth of the world's oil goes through that water in an ordinary year. Nobody in those rooms is talking in weeks."

I just stood there.

"That's why Daniel and the girls are in my spare rooms. That's why the boat's gone. That's why there's a stove coming Thursday."

"All right. So what do I do?"

He looked at me a while. Then he sort of laughed. A worn out laugh.

"Tell you the truth, everything I just listed is the easy part."

"Easy?"

"It's what your nan would've done without anybody telling her. Anybody who lived through the three-day week. None of it takes inside knowledge. It's chores."

"You sold a boat you loved, Graham. Don't stand there and tell me that's chores."

"It is to the people who know."

I didn't answer him.

"None of that is what has me up at three in the morning."

"Then what does."

Long drink of tea.

"Something that came up about a month in. One slide, in a room I only got into because somebody was off sick. They spent four minutes on it and moved on. I'd give up every box in that shed before I'd give up my answer to it."

"Your answer to what?"

He looked right at me.

"The radio."

"The radio?"

"When this gets bad, knowing what's going on is the whole game. Ahead of cash. Ahead of a full tank. Ahead of that log pile."

"The radio."

"You can be cold a good while. You can get through a dark house with candles. But the day the phones go, you're on your own. And you won't even know how on your own you are. You won't know if it's your street or the whole country. You won't know if your daughter's all right. You won't know where to go or when it's coming back."

"Go how."

"Spain and Portugal. 28th of April last year. The whole grid went, both countries. Tens of millions of people. No trains, no metro, no traffic lights, no cash machines, no phones, no internet. Card payments didn't work. The mobiles stopped and nobody had any information. Some places were sixteen hours with no power. The ones who knew it was the whole country and not just their road were the ones sat next to a battery radio."

"But we've got our mobiles."

"The phones go too. Nobody ever sees that one coming."

"Graham."

"Your mobile works because the mast at the end of the road has power. Mast loses power, it runs on its backup for a few hours if you're lucky. Then nothing. Your landline? They've switched you to digital. It goes through the router. The router's on the mains. Ofcom says the battery backup only has to last 'at least one hour.' And the old copper line, the one that worked in a power cut, gets switched off on the 31st of January. It's on gov.uk. Look it up."

"Storm Arwen, November 2021. Over a million homes lost power. Nearly four thousand were off for more than a week. Up in Aberdeenshire and Northumberland the masts went with the power. No landline, no mobile, no leccy. People sat in freezing houses for days not knowing when anybody was coming."

"A week."

"Over a week. From one storm. Storm Éowyn, January last year, 285,000 homes and businesses in Northern Ireland, and NIE told some of them they could be waiting till the 3rd of February. Berlin, this January. Somebody set fire to the power cables. Five days, in the freezing cold, about a hundred thousand people. Czech Republic, the summer before last, half a million off and about a thousand mobile masts running on backup. Heathrow, one fire at one substation, and the busiest airport in Europe shut for the day."

"Every one of those was one place at a time. With the rest of the country standing by to send help."

"What I'm telling you about is everywhere at once. And nobody's standing by, because everybody's in it."

He set his mug on the fence post.

"Picture it. Day three. Your grandkids are frightened. It's pitch dark at half four. The phone says No Service. The telly's off, the internet's off. Your daughter's on the other side of town and you don't know if she's all right, and she doesn't know if you are. And you're stood in your kitchen with a candle trying to work out if it's your road or the whole of Britain."

"Don't."

"I know. I'm sorry. But that's the one that gets me up at night. Everybody's staring at the petrol pump. Nobody's looking at the phone in their hand."

"This can't be right."

"Ask yourself why every headline says oil and not one of them says phones. The Department of Health put it on gov.uk in black and white. In a national power outage, phone, internet and television services would be disrupted, so emergency communications to the public would be limited to radio. BBC Radio 2 and Radio 4. That's it. Now walk down this road and count how many houses have a radio that works without the mains. They won't say it out loud, because the minute they do, there won't be a wind-up radio left in the country by teatime. That's what 'avoiding a panic' means."

"All right. So what are you doing about it?"

He looked at his mug.

"We're sorted."

"What's that mean."

"Means we're sorted."

"Graham."

"I'd rather leave it there."

"You haven't left one thing there in twenty minutes."

Nothing.

"Graham. You've just stood my granddaughter in my kitchen in the pitch dark. You do not get to say that to me and go back to chopping logs."

He looked at me a long moment.

"It's not something I'm meant to be passing round."

"Passing what round."

"What people in my line of work are doing at their own houses."

"Tell me."

He sighed. Looked at the shed. Looked at the logs. Looked back at me.

"There's an item. One particular item. Everybody I trust in this business has them. The chap who runs our control room up north. A woman on my team who did twenty years in the Royal Navy before she came to us. My boss ordered ten back in the spring, for his kids and the caravan, when all anybody else was buying was jerry cans."

"What item."

"It's small. It's cheap, considering. It's no secret, you could look it up tonight. It's just that nobody outside my little world has tied it to any of this yet."

"Graham. What is it."

One more long look.

Then: "Stay there."

He went in his shed. Came back out with something in his hand.

Red. About the size of a mobile phone. A black handle folded flat on the back. A silver aerial.

He held it up.

"This."

"A radio?"

"An emergency radio. AM and FM. You wind it with that crank, or you leave it on the windowsill and the little solar panel on top does it, or you plug it into USB-C while the power's still on. Torch on the end. SOS alarm. And a 2000 mAh battery inside it that'll put charge back into your phone. No socket. No batteries to go flat in a drawer."

"And that's what..."

"That's what we've all got. There's one in Linda's glovebox, she just doesn't know what it is. One in each of the girls' rucksacks. That's the item."

"That little thing."

"That's why it works. Goes in a handbag. Needs no mains and no batteries. And nobody can switch it off."

"Graham, does that thing actually work?"

"I'll let you answer that yourself in about five minutes. Go and get your phone."

I went and got it. Nine per cent, because it's always nine per cent. Followed him round the back of his house.

He opened the cupboard under his stairs where the fuse box is.

Flicked the main switch.

The whole house went. The fridge stopped humming. The router light by the telly went out. Somewhere upstairs Daniel shouted "Dad!"

He took my phone off me. Turned the Wi-Fi on. Nothing to connect to. One bar, the way it always is in that hallway.

Then he put the radio in my hand.

"Wind it."

"Graham."

"Wind it."

"You go first."

That got a real grin out of him. He took it back, turned the crank a good few times and handed it back.

I clicked it on. Pushed it to FM. Turned the dial.

I was braced for hiss.

It was Radio 4. Clear as anything. A man reading the shipping forecast in a house with no electricity.

"Well, I'll be."

"That's all there is to it."

He pressed the button on the end. The torch lit the whole hallway, right up the stairs.

Then he took the cable out of his pocket, plugged my phone into the side of the radio, and the little charging symbol came up on my screen.

Then he pressed the SOS.

It nearly took my ears off. Linda shouted something from the garden I won't repeat.

"And it does that with no power at all?"

"No power at all. Crank, sun, or the battery inside. Whatever the grid's doing."

"And what's it pick up."

"AM and FM. The BBC keeps FM going when everything else goes. That's the whole point of FM. It works almost everywhere."

I stood there holding it in the dark.

"Graham, where do you even get one."

"Same place everybody I work with got theirs. I'll write it down for you."

He flicked the power back on. The fridge started up again. He put the radio in my hand.

"Keep that one. I've got a box of them. I'll leave you some tomorrow. Give them to your kids. Tell them it's from their mother and she'll sleep better. Leave me out of it. They don't have to believe a word of this. They just have to have it in a drawer on the day."

"Graham."

"Forget the log burner if you want. Forget the cash and every other thing I said. I wouldn't. But you could. This one you can't skip."

"All right."

"When the lights go and everybody on this road is sat in the dark refreshing a phone with no signal, the woman with one of these on her windowsill knows what's going on. There's a word I keep landing on for that. Free. Whatever they switch off, it stops at the edge of that radio."

"Most folk are going to hear about all this on the six o'clock news. That's a week too late, and it's assuming the telly's working. You're hearing it from me, today, over a fence. Do something with it."

He went back to his log pile.

I went inside. Put it in the kitchen drawer next to the batteries. Told myself Graham had sat in too many meetings.

I left it there two days.

Then I sat down with my iPad and started checking up on him.

The National Security Strategy really does say we must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK homeland coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario." June 2025. It names Russia, Iran, China and North Korea.

The National Risk Register 2026 really does have a national power outage on it. Rated catastrophic. "All consumers without backup generators would lose their mains electricity supply instantaneously and without warning." Instantaneously. And without warning.

The Department of Health really did write that emergency communications would be limited to radio. Radio 2 and Radio 4. "The most power resilient form of communication."

The copper landline really does get switched off on the 31st of January 2027.

And the government's own Be Ready checklist, the one they want every household to have, really does say "FM radio (battery / wind up)." Right there between the torch and the power bank.

Every single thing Graham said checked out.

Then I looked up Storm Arwen. Over a million customers. Nearly four thousand off for over a week.

Just like he said.

Graham left a carrier bag hanging on my back door handle the next morning. Didn't knock. Four more of them inside.

I rang my daughter that afternoon and said I was coming over.

I gave her two. One for her kitchen, one for her husband's van. She said, "Mum, I'm not a prepper." I said neither am I, love.

I drove to my son's and gave him two. One for the house, one for the changing bag.

The one from the fence stayed in my kitchen drawer.

My son gave me the look. Same one he's been giving me since he was fifteen.

Doesn't bother me one bit.

If you've had a feeling for a while now that something is off, that the news keeps walking round something without ever saying it, you are not going mad.

The people who deal with this for a living have already sorted their own houses. Quietly. No announcement.

Graham had one thing dead right. By the time it's on the six o'clock news, the shelf is already bare. The person sat in the dark is the person who heard last.

This is the same radio Graham handed me over the fence. I've put the link below.

I'm not a prepper. I'm a nan with a kitchen drawer. But when the lights go and the phones go with them, I'd like to be the woman who sorted it back in October.

The last thing your family will hear before the grid fails is nothing. No warning. No siren. No announcement. Just the moment the lights go out and every device in the house goes quiet at the same second. I know this because I maintain the civilian grid. I have maintained it for 26 years. And the UK's National Security Strategy, published on 24 June 2025, said that for the first time in many years Britain must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK homeland coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario". They are not worried about the dark. They are worried about the silence that comes after it.

My name is Gareth. I am 52. Master electrician. Twenty-six years with a regional utility in the Midlands. I do not read about the grid. I open the panels. I test the load. I file quarterly condition assessments. And I need to tell you something about those assessments that the government's own papers now say in plain English — not about power. About what you lose when the power stops.

Most people think a grid failure means the lights go out. That is the first thing that happens. It is not the dangerous thing. The dangerous thing is what goes dark in the hours after the lights — the things you did not know were connected to the same system.

Your phone connects to a mobile mast. That mast runs on the grid. The government's Be Ready pages say your mobile might stop working if your local mast is in the affected area. In the most serious circumstances your mobile, landline and broadband could all be down. Every phone in your house. Every phone on your street. Every phone in your town. Quiet at the same hour.

Your television connects through a box connected to a router connected to the wall. Same grid. Same failure. Same hour. gov.uk Be Ready says that in a power cut your TV or internet might not be working.

Your laptop connects through the same router. Same grid. Same silence.

Your kid's tablet. Your wife's watch. The doorbell camera. The baby monitor. The smart speaker your daughter asks questions to before bed. Every single thing in your house that connects your family to the outside world runs through the same grid the National Risk Register 2026 calls a "Catastrophic" national power outage: "All consumers without backup generators would lose their mains electricity supply instantaneously and without warning."

I have been filing this in my reports for years. Not the technical language — the human language. I write about cascade failures and single-point vulnerabilities and fuel-chain dependencies. But what I am actually writing about is silence. Every report I have filed for 26 years is a description of how fast your family loses contact with the outside world when the system I maintain stops working.

The Department of Health and Social Care put the human part in writing on 16 December 2025. In a national power outage, "phone, internet and television services would be disrupted." For that reason, "emergency communications to the public would be limited to radio (BBC Radio 2 and Radio 4), which is the most power resilient form of communication." Radio. Because the people who wrote that understand what most families do not — the most dangerous thing about a grid failure is not what stops working. It is what stops talking.

I told my wife on a Wednesday.

Not about transformers. Not about substations. I sat across from her at the kitchen table and I said: "Helen, I need to tell you something about the house."

"What about the house?"

"Everything in this house that tells you what is happening outside — the phone, the TV, the laptop, the tablet — all of it connects through the same grid. The grid I maintain. When the grid fails, you lose all of it. Not as a rumour. The National Risk Register says the loss is instantaneous and without warning. About 60% of demand reconnected within 2 days. Beyond 7 days they expect full and stable power restored to all of Great Britain. Until then you are sitting in this kitchen with the kids and you do not know if there is a flood warning or an evacuation order or a chemical spill south of Coventry. You do not know if the schools are closed. You do not know if the motorway is open. You do not know anything. Because every way you find things out runs through the same system that just died."

She looked at her phone on the counter. I have seen that look before. I saw it on my mum's face. On my neighbour's face. The look of someone seeing a permanent thing as temporary for the first time. The phone sits on the counter like a fixture. Like a tap. Like a light switch. It is not a fixture. It is rented — from a mast, from a grid, from a fuel tanker, from a strait.

"So how do I know what is happening?"

"Right now you do not."

She sat with that for a long time. Then she said something that stayed with me for days.
